In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and application of novel causal modeling techniques to the problem of estimating the effects of a particular modifiable intermediate variable (weight gain) on the risk of premature death.
the estimation of the effects of weight on mortality in the presence of reverse causation and unmeasured confounders.

the estimation of the effects of a time-dependent treatment (weight gain) on an outcome (mortality) in a population (18-year old men) that is exposed to a time-dependent treatment that can be controlled by a health policy intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the presence of a large HMO with electronic records of all members, our proposed g-estimation approach is the only method capable of providing an unbiased estimate of the effect of weight gain on all-cause mortality in the absence of unmeasured confounders.

, in the context of a large HMO with a large number of subjects, the g-estimation approach to SNMs is the only method that can be used to adjust for all three sources of bias, and, in the absence or model misspecification (which is difficult to test), is likely to provide the best possible unbiased estimate of the effect of weight gain on death.

the g-estimation of the SNM can be used with confidence to estimate the effect of weight gain on death in a population in which the SNM is correct, and that the other g-methods are useful in estimating the effect of weight change in populations where the SNM may not be correct.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SNM is a useful tool in causal inference, but its use should be accompanied by a clear understanding of its limitations.

we have developed a method for estimating the effects on mortality of weight gain in a population of non-smoking men that is not confounded by the effects of exercise, hypertension, diabetes and other measured time-varyng confounders, and that is robust against the effects of unmeasured confounders due to undiagnosed disease and the effects of particular identifiable subpopulations in which confounding by unobserved variables is so severe as render the method infeasible.

the SNM is a very flexible and useful model for estimating the effect of a modifiable exposure on a binary outcome when the exposure is subject to a time-varying treatment policy and when the outcome is subject to a competing risk of death.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in contrast to conventional epidemiological analyses, which are based upon the assumption that the observed data are sufficient to estimate the effects of weight on mortality, we can now estimate the effects of counterfactual weight gain on mortality using only longitudinal epidemiologic data.

it is now possible to empirically test the causal hypothesis that weight gain causes death by using the SNM to estimate the counterfactual contrast of interest and then testing whether the SNM adequately adjusts for the bias due to (ii).
it is now possible to use longitudinal epidemiologic data to empirically test the hypothesis that weight gain is causally related to increased risk of mortality.
